item.title: Infraspinatus Region — Gentle Trigger Point Compression
clinicalUse: A swimmer says reaching across the body feels sore, and gentle palpation of the posterior scapular region reproduces a familiar local discomfort. A tender spot is a clue, not the diagnosis.
Consider a short, tolerable local compression trial only alongside shoulder evaluation and functional exercise.
Identify a safe repeated baseline such as controlled shoulder external rotation or reaching behind the back.
patientPosition: Side-lying with the treated shoulder uppermost, or prone with the shoulder and arm comfortably supported.
Support the head, scapula and arm; avoid positioning that aggravates an unstable or acutely inflamed shoulder.
therapistPosition: Stand beside the scapula with relaxed shoulders, forearm support where possible and a neutral wrist.
Maintain clear access to the posterior scapular surface without leaning your full body weight on a small contact point.
stabilization: Support the arm so the posterior shoulder musculature need not guard against gravity.
Use broad contact to steady the area near the infraspinous fossa, remaining away from the axilla.
contact: Palpate the infraspinatus muscle belly over the infraspinous scapular fossa, inferior to the scapular spine, with a supported thumb pad or finger pads.
Do not compress the axilla, suprascapular notch or other neurovascular areas; avoid painful bony contact.
forceDirection: Introduce gradually increasing, stationary, comfortable pressure toward the soft tissue supported by the scapula, without forceful digging.
Ask whether the pressure reproduces a familiar, tolerable sensation; radiating electrical pain or numbness is not an acceptable target.
dosage: Begin with a brief 15–30-second monitored trial, adjusting or ending earlier as needed; specific optimal dosing is not established.
Pressure is titrated to comfort and clinical response. More pain does not mean more effective release.
steps: Check the familiar shoulder movement and screen for rotator-cuff tear, acute injury, cervical referral or neurological features as appropriate.
Position the patient with the arm supported and identify the infraspinatus muscle region anatomically.
Apply broad supported contact first, then a small amount of steady, tolerable pressure over the selected muscular area.
Ask for feedback and adjust immediately for guarding, symptom spread or discomfort; do not chase high pain scores.
Release slowly and let the shoulder settle.
Repeat the same shoulder rotation/reach and measure whether anything useful changed.
Link any improvement to graded external-rotation control or other relevant functional exercise.
reassess: Reach behind the back or across the body
mistakes: Calling every tender area a validated active trigger point or the sole cause of shoulder symptoms.
Digging forcefully with a thumb near vulnerable scapular borders.
Ignoring changes in the neck or arm simply because pressure on the scapula reproduces discomfort.
safety: Do not use sustained compression over suspected acute tear, local infection, fracture, hematoma or damaged skin.
Stop for numbness, electric shock sensations, worsening radiating pain or disproportionate discomfort.
Screen referred pain and neurological signs before treating a small tender region as a stand-alone diagnosis.
item.visualCue: Posterior scapula/infraspinous fossa → tolerable static muscular pressure → retest active shoulder rotation.

story.title: The tiny tender spot with a huge reputation
story.scene: A swimmer points to the back of the shoulder. Pressing one region of the infraspinatus reproduces familiar discomfort. That is a clue, but the rotator cuff, neck and movement pattern have not left the story.
story.clinicalDecision: The arm is supported while the clinician uses a measured, stationary contact over the infraspinous muscle belly. Pressure stays tolerable. If the sensation becomes electric or spreads unexpectedly, the therapist stops—no medal is awarded for 'deepest thumb'.
story.retest: The swimmer repeats comfortable rotation. If symptoms improve, the clinician builds toward controlled cuff loading. If not, the tender spot has not won the right to explain the entire problem.
story.punchline: A sore spot is a witness, not the judge.
story.evidenceCaveat: Local compression may modify pain briefly, but tender-point palpation alone is not a definitive diagnosis. Specific dose and lasting effects remain uncertain.
